newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem refugees seek hope at Bosnia rally.
newsitem.headline: Moslem refugees seek hope at Bosnia rally.

text.p: Some came just for free entertainment but most of the 2,000 people who gathered for an election rally of Bosnia's main Moslem nationalist party had come to hear a promise of a better future.

Refugees from around Bosnia, now settled in other people's houses, streamed on Saturday evening to a political rally promoting the Moslem SDA party in a miserable Sarajevo suburb just coming to life after Bosnian Serbs vacated it in March.
Hollow-eyed and dressed in ill-fitting clothes, Ibrahim Mulaomerovic fixed his gaze at a brightly-lit stage, decorated with green-and-white SDA flags.
"I want to go back to my home. I came to hear a promise that I will," said the 56-year-old refugee from a village 30 km (20 miles) southeast of Sarajevo.
Popular folk tunes echoed loudly from the crumbling sports hall, bristling with SDA flags, and invited fun-starved residents of Ilidza suburb for a rare occasion to sing.
Teenagers chanted "Alija, Alija" after hearing the name of Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic during a speech of a local politician which otherwise did nothing to rouse them.
"I've never seen Alija (Izetbegovic) alive," Haris, 16, said excitedly even though the president's attendance was not officially planned. He did not show up.
"But the music was worth coming for as well," said Haris.
Countrywide elections have been set for September 14 under the terms of the 1995 Dayton peace agreement which ended 43 months of fighting.

Envisioned as patching back together a country divided among Moslems, Serbs and Croats, the elections are likely to fall short of the goal and only strengthen the grip of the ruling nationalist parties, analysts say.

While Bosnian Serbs and Croats openly advocate secession and merger with Serbia and Croatia proper, Moslem-led parties are officially promoting multi-ethnic life and play on refugee votes, demanding they be allowed to return to their homes.
The SDA rally played Bosnia's national anthem, but each speaker began with solely Islamic greetings. Foreign television cameras searched the crowd for an Islamic presence and found it.
A group of young men chanted "Allahu Akbar," (Arabic for "God is Great"), after an imam (Moslem priest) said a prayer for the war dead.

Speakers urged people to remember the SDA was with them during the war against separatist Serbs, Croats and rebel Moslems. One said: "Whatever wrong was done, we've done it, but whatever good was done, we've done it too."
"I believe only in Alija (Izetbegovic) because he was with us throughout the war," said Mustafa, a 33-year-old former Bosnian army soldier, waving the SDA flag in the din.
"It's only fair that I vote for him."

Prospects for the return of refugees have dimmed further since Serb police in late August beat up a group of Moslems repairing their houses in a northeastern village which they abandoned during the war.
"One can only hope. It's easier to hope if you hear a promise," Mulaomerovic sighed.
